Live Free or Die; Giving Testimony in New Hampshire By Denis Cicero of The Galaxy Global Eatery

From the May Issue of Hemp Magazine
See HEMP DINING IN THE STARS A Restaurant Review
and
Learning Important Lessons from Bad Journalism in An Article Supposedly About Hemp
and

Martha’s Vineyard, 1976:

We were in the café of my first restaurant, eating crepes made with flour and round cannabis seed. Each person’s testimony swirled hither to and fro primarily centering on the conclusion of the Vietnam War and its relationship to societal thinking as a whole. Iconoclasm was in vogue. The question to answer was, "How do you influence society on the basic tenants of ‘living free’ without threatening the stability of society as we know it?" I don’t remember any earth shattering results from our cerebral frothing other than the excitement of being under the stars with those in six degrees of separation bonded by the most singular of all important events: GIVING TESTIMONY!

February 3, 1998:

Sitting on a Delta shuttle from New York City to Manchester, New "Hempshire", across from Hemp Times publisher John Howell, a sense of despair overwhelmed me. Are we chasing our tails? Is the system larger than we are? Can we effectively chase these blue suits from the podium and re-educate the American public about the industrial and nutritional applications of hemp? Is it worth the personal expense of time and money to butt heads with a government who doesn’t even blink at spending billions in order to safeguard their right to say NO? Looking out the plane’s window, I could see Martha’s Vineyard where, 20 years ago, I stood on the beach, insisting that all of my brethren never give up the will and determination to give testimony to those elements of the soul that allow us to "Live free or die".

Two hours later, John and I arrived at the Legislative Office Building in Concord, New Hampshire for the Agricultural subcommittee hearing on NH House bill 1576 (legalization of industrial hemp). The findings from this hearing would be given to the full committee of the Environment and Agriculture for review. Some noble countrymen, among them Karl Bond and Mark Lathrop, co-chairmen of the NH Hemp Council, had invited us.

Despair raised its ugly head again as I listened to the DEA’s official misrepresent the facts time and time again. Was this trip worth it? Will we even get a chance to speak? Does it ultimately matter anyway? I revisited that cool breeze from the North Atlantic jarring my mind to a full moon night on the Vineyard when idealism and iconoclasm were one and the same.

NEXT: "MR. CICERO" the chairman announced. What was supposed to be a five-minute testimony became a 25 minute lecture. The panel was captivated about hemp, in particular about the nutraceutical side of the issue since this is one area none of these congressmen were even remotely associated with. There was some familiarity with rope, fabric and lubricating oil, but FOOD? NUTRITION?

I gave them the short version of protein analysis, EFA’S, GLA, arterial plaque, blood pressure and referred them to authors such as Udo Erasmus, Kenneth Jones and Chris Conrad. I even offered to cater their next hearing with edible hemp products including some of The Galaxy’s Hemp Vanilla coffee.

I then showed them PRODUCT in the form of hempnut, coffee and hemp seed oil, substantiating the reality of an industry already in motion in food production. I also promised to invest $100,000 in a hempseed oil and de-hulling plant on a farm owned by the descendants of former Governor Prescott. Many eyebrows were raised as the letter of intent from the Prescott estate was placed into public record.

I continued to drive home the economics of republicanism: MONEY AND JOBS. "I want to come to your state and create jobs, infuse money into your economy, and resurrect your old textile mills, bakeries and oil processing plants no matter the scale. I am willing and able to invest in your state to build a new industry in farming and food production. But you must lose your fears and open your minds to the soil that makes all things good." We talked about phytoremediation, crop rotation, pesticides, herbicides and toxic water tables. We talked about their bordering neighbor, Canada, competing for their jobs and building their own hempen economy a few hours to the north.

When all was said and done, the committee voted 5-2 not to recommend the bill to the full committee. Despair laughed me back to the airplane, mocking our efforts as we landed in the Big Apple. Two weeks later, with help from Amy Robb-Theroux (D, Sullivan County) and Peter R. Leishman (R, Hillsboro County), the bill passed the committee by a vote of 10-8 and was sent to the full house floor for a vote. WOW!!

TESTIMONY. Apparently the committee members who were moved by our words took heed and arm wrangled the bill to the floor after only our first attempt at educating the legislature. Needless to say, the debate was fierce and heated. In the end, the bill was defeated by a vote of 175 nay to 164 yea, only an 11 vote margin, with 58 absentees.

Lessons to be learned:

1) A small group of people can make a difference with a concerted effort to educate.

2) Avoid the controversy of marijuana. Medicinal marijuana should not be linked to industrial hemp legislation

3) Show product and job development.

4) Connect to the mainstream part of the population.

5) Do not despair! The truth will prevail. Give Testimony!

LIVE FREE OR DIE!

Hempfully humble,

Denis Cicero
The Galaxy Global Eatery
15 Irving Place, New York City
